name: Calcium
summary: Calcium is the main mineral in bones and teeth, and the body also needs it for muscles, nerves and blood clotting. The body keeps the blood level steady by taking calcium from bone when intake is low. Trials of calcium supplements found small effects on bone density, weak and inconsistent effects on fractures, and some possible harms.
roles: Builds and maintains bones and teeth (about 99% of the body's calcium is there)
Release of hormones and other messengers from cells

status.note: There is no simple test of calcium intake, and this app has no calcium marker. Blood calcium is kept in a narrow range by hormones (parathyroid hormone and vitamin D), which draw calcium from bone when intake is low, so a normal blood calcium does not show that intake is enough. A doctor may check blood calcium (often adjusted for albumin), parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, or bone density with a DXA scan (a low-dose X-ray). These show problems with calcium balance or bone health, not how much calcium someone eats.

signs: Low intake usually causes no symptoms at first, because calcium is taken from bone
Over years: lower bone density and a higher chance of osteoporosis
Low blood calcium (hypocalcaemia), usually from hormone, vitamin D or kidney problems rather than diet: tingling around the mouth or in the fingers, muscle cramps and spasms
atRisk: People who eat no dairy and no calcium-fortified alternatives (for example some vegans, or people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy)
People with low vitamin D, which reduces calcium absorption
Women after menopause, who lose bone faster
Older adults, who absorb calcium less well
People with coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease or after weight-loss surgery
Populations with low calcium diets, which are common in many low- and middle-income countries

signs: Constipation, bloating and wind (common with supplements)
Too much calcium in the blood (hypercalcaemia): nausea, thirst, passing a lot of urine, tiredness, confusion
Milk-alkali syndrome: high calcium, kidney problems and alkaline blood from large amounts of calcium carbonate, often as antacids
high.note: High blood calcium from food alone is rare. It happens mainly with supplements or calcium-containing antacids, especially together with high amounts of vitamin D, or because of a medical condition (overactive parathyroid glands, some cancers). In the Women's Health Initiative trial, calcium with vitamin D raised the risk of kidney stones.

examples: Tofu set with calcium (calcium sulphate or calcium chloride)
Canned fish eaten with the soft bones, such as sardines, pilchards and salmon
Green vegetables such as kale, pak choi, spring greens and broccoli
Bread and other foods made with calcium-fortified flour (white flour in the UK is fortified)
Hard tap water and some mineral waters
foodSources.note: How much calcium the body absorbs differs between foods. Oxalate (in spinach and rhubarb) and phytate (in bran and some seeds) bind calcium, so spinach supplies far less usable calcium than its content suggests.

forms.name: Calcium carbonate
forms.note: The most common and cheapest form, with about 40% calcium by weight. It needs stomach acid, so it is absorbed best with food. It is also the active ingredient of many antacids, which count towards total intake.

forms.name: Calcium citrate
forms.note: About 21% calcium, so tablets are larger or more numerous. It is absorbed with or without food and is often preferred for people with low stomach acid or on acid-reducing medicines.

forms.name: Calcium lactate and gluconate
forms.note: Contain much less calcium per gram, so they are less practical as supplements.

forms.name: Hydroxyapatite, algae, coral or bone-derived calcium
forms.note: Marketed as natural forms. Research on how well they work is limited.

forms.name: Calcium with vitamin D
forms.note: Most fracture trials used combined products. The label's 'elemental calcium' is the amount of calcium itself, not the weight of the whole compound. The body absorbs a larger share of smaller amounts, so a large amount at once is absorbed less efficiently.

intake.group: Adults 25 years and over (men and women)
Pregnancy or breastfeeding, 25 years and over

upperLimit.note: From food and supplements together, for adults including during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Set by the EU's Scientific Committee on Food in 2003 and confirmed by EFSA (the European Food Safety Authority) in 2012, because long trials found total intakes of 2500 mg a day were tolerated without harm. EFSA keeps the same intake value in pregnancy and breastfeeding because the body adapts its handling of calcium during these times.

findings.population: Adults over 50, mostly women after menopause; some trials in care-home residents
whyThisGrade: Many randomised trials, but results differ between them
Trials at the lowest risk of bias found no effect at any site
Signs of publication bias favouring calcium
The clearest benefit came from frail people in care homes with low calcium and vitamin D
findings.summary: Pooled trials of calcium supplements (with or without vitamin D) found about 11% fewer fractures overall, but the best-quality trials found none, and a review of trials in older adults living at home found no lower fracture risk with calcium, vitamin D or both. Combined with vitamin D, the Cochrane review found a small drop in hip fractures, mainly in care-home residents. The large Women's Health Initiative trial (1000 mg calcium with 400 IU vitamin D a day) did not significantly reduce hip fractures.
findings.bottomLine: In adults over 50, calcium supplements with or without vitamin D cut fractures by about 11% in pooled trials, but the best-quality trials found no drop. With vitamin D, a small fall in hip fractures was seen mainly in care homes.
findings.label: Bone fractures
findings.line: About 11% fewer in pooled trials of adults over 50, but no drop in the best-quality trials

whyThisGrade: Over 50 randomised trials with consistent results
Bone density is a stand-in measure, not fractures themselves
The increase is small and does not grow over time
findings.summary: Calcium supplements raised bone density by about 1 to 2% at most sites. The gain appeared in the first year and did not grow after that, and the reviewers judged it unlikely to reduce fractures in a meaningful way. A higher number on a scan is not the same as fewer broken bones.
findings.bottomLine: In adults over 50, calcium supplements raised bone density by about 1 to 2%, mostly in the first year. Reviewers judged a gain this small unlikely to reduce fractures in a meaningful way.
findings.label: Bone density
findings.line: Raised bone density by about 1 to 2%, judged too small to cut fractures much

findings.population: Older adults, mostly women after menopause
whyThisGrade: Meta-analyses of the same kind of trials reached different conclusions
Heart events were not the main outcome of most trials and were often self-reported
A later analysis using only verified heart events found no increase
findings.summary: Meta-analyses by Bolland and colleagues found about 20 to 30% more heart attacks with calcium supplements, with or without vitamin D. A later meta-analysis that counted only heart events confirmed from medical records found no increase in heart disease or deaths. Whether calcium supplements raise heart risk is still debated. EFSA concluded in 2012 that no link with cardiovascular disease had been established.
findings.bottomLine: In older adults, mostly women after menopause, some meta-analyses found about 20 to 30% more heart attacks with calcium supplements, but one using events confirmed from medical records found no increase. Whether calcium raises heart risk is still debated.
findings.label: Heart attacks and strokes
findings.line: Some reviews found 20 to 30% more heart attacks, another no increase; still debated

findings.population: Women after menopause; older adults in fracture trials
whyThisGrade: Mainly one large randomised trial, where calcium was given with vitamin D
Supported by more kidney problems in the Cochrane review of vitamin D with or without calcium
EFSA judged in 2012 that a link at intakes up to the upper limit had not been established
findings.summary: In the Women's Health Initiative trial, women taking 1000 mg calcium with 400 IU vitamin D a day had about 17% more kidney stones over 7 years. The Cochrane review of vitamin D with or without calcium found about 16% more kidney disease. Calcium from food did not show this pattern (see the food findings).
findings.bottomLine: In women after menopause, 1000 mg calcium with 400 IU vitamin D a day led to about 17% more kidney stones over 7 years in the Women's Health Initiative trial. Calcium from food did not show this pattern.
findings.label: Kidney stones
findings.line: About 17% more over 7 years with calcium plus vitamin D in a large trial of women after menopause

findings.outcome: Pre-eclampsia and high blood pressure in pregnancy
findings.population: Pregnant women, especially those with low calcium diets
whyThisGrade: 27 randomised trials with over 18,000 women
Rated low-quality evidence for pre-eclampsia by the Cochrane authors
Results differ a lot between trials, and small trials showed bigger effects (possible publication bias)
In the largest trial the reduction was only 8% and could have been chance
findings.summary: Calcium supplements in pregnancy (trials used at least 1 g a day) were linked to less high blood pressure and pre-eclampsia, a serious pregnancy complication. The effect was clear in women with low calcium diets but not in women whose diets already had enough. HELLP syndrome, a rare complication, was slightly more common with calcium. This is a decision for the pregnancy care team, not a general rule.
findings.bottomLine: In pregnant women, calcium supplements (at least 1 g a day in trials) were linked to less high blood pressure and pre-eclampsia, but clearly only in women with low calcium diets. A rare complication, HELLP syndrome, was slightly more common.
findings.label: Pre-eclampsia (pregnancy)
findings.line: Less high blood pressure and pre-eclampsia, clearly only in women with low-calcium diets

studies.title: Calcium supplementation during pregnancy for preventing hypertensive disorders and related problems

findings.population: Adults who recently had adenomas removed
whyThisGrade: One large, well-run, double-blind randomised trial
Follow-up of only 3 to 5 years
Adenomas are a step towards bowel cancer, not cancer itself
findings.summary: Calcium (1200 mg a day), vitamin D (1000 IU a day) or both did not lower the number of people whose adenomas came back over 3 to 5 years.
findings.bottomLine: In adults who recently had bowel polyps removed, calcium (1200 mg a day), vitamin D (1000 IU a day) or both did not lower the number of people whose polyps came back over 3 to 5 years.
findings.label: Bowel polyps coming back
findings.line: Did not lower how many people had polyps come back over 3 to 5 years

studies.title: A Trial of Calcium and Vitamin D for the Prevention of Colorectal Adenomas

foodFindings.outcome: Bone fractures (calcium, milk and dairy from food)
foodFindings.population: Adults over 50 in 44 cohort studies; only 2 small trials
whyThisGrade: Mostly observational studies, which can't prove cause
Results were consistent: most studies found no link
Almost no randomised trials of food calcium with fractures as the outcome
foodFindings.summary: In most cohort studies, people who ate more calcium, milk or dairy did not have fewer fractures. There is no trial evidence that eating more calcium-rich food prevents fractures.
foodFindings.bottomLine: In 44 cohort studies of adults over 50, people who ate more calcium, milk or dairy mostly did not have fewer fractures. There is no trial evidence that eating more calcium-rich food prevents fractures.
foodFindings.label: Calcium-rich food: fractures
foodFindings.line: People eating more calcium, milk or dairy mostly didn't have fewer fractures

foodFindings.outcome: Bone mineral density (more calcium from food)
whyThisGrade: Randomised trials, but fewer and smaller than for supplements (about 1500 people)
Bone density is a stand-in measure, not fractures
The increase was small
foodFindings.summary: Adding calcium-rich foods raised bone density by about 1 to 2%, similar to supplements. As with supplements, a gain this small is unlikely to change fracture risk much.
foodFindings.bottomLine: In 15 trials of adults over 50, adding calcium-rich foods raised bone density by about 1 to 2%, similar to supplements. As with supplements, a gain this small is unlikely to change fracture risk much.
foodFindings.label: Calcium-rich food: bone density
foodFindings.line: Adding calcium-rich foods raised bone density by about 1 to 2%, like supplements

studies.title: Calcium intake and bone mineral density: systematic review and meta-analysis

foodFindings.outcome: Kidney stones (calcium from food compared with supplements)
whyThisGrade: One large observational study, which can't prove cause
Other parts of dairy foods, or other habits, may explain part of the link
The opposite pattern for supplements fits the randomised Women's Health Initiative result
foodFindings.summary: Women with the most calcium from food had about 35% fewer kidney stones than those with the least, while women using calcium supplements had about 20% more. One explanation is that calcium eaten with meals binds oxalate in the gut. This is a good example of why food and supplements are treated as different things.
foodFindings.bottomLine: In 91,731 US nurses followed for 12 years, those with the most calcium from food had about 35% fewer kidney stones, while those using calcium supplements had about 20% more. Food and supplements behaved differently here.
foodFindings.label: Food calcium: kidney stones
foodFindings.line: In US nurses: about 35% fewer stones with the most food calcium, 20% more with supplements

studies.title: Comparison of dietary calcium with supplemental calcium and other nutrients as factors affecting the risk for kidney stones in women

interactions.note: Calcium and phosphate balance changes in kidney disease and is usually managed by the kidney team; some phosphate binders contain calcium and count towards intake. Talk to your doctor before using calcium supplements.
EFSA's intake value is the same in pregnancy. Calcium to lower the risk of pre-eclampsia is a decision for the midwife or doctor, and the evidence is strongest for low calcium diets.
In a small study, calcium carbonate taken together with levothyroxine lowered thyroid hormone levels and raised TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone). Pharmacists usually advise keeping them hours apart.

interactions.with: Some antibiotics (tetracyclines such as doxycycline, quinolones such as ciprofloxacin)
interactions.note: Calcium binds these antibiotics in the gut and makes them work less well if taken at the same time.
Calcium blocks their absorption when taken together; the leaflet explains the timing.
Calcium taken at the same time can reduce iron absorption.

interactions.with: Thiazide diuretics (water tablets such as bendroflumethiazide)
interactions.note: They reduce calcium lost in urine, so high calcium intake can raise blood calcium.
Vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium. High amounts of both together raise the chance of high blood calcium and kidney stones.
They count towards total calcium intake; large amounts over time can cause milk-alkali syndrome.

cautions: Check the elemental calcium on the label: that is the amount that counts, not the weight of the compound.
Count calcium from food, fortified foods, antacids and supplements together against the upper limit.
Many medicines need to be kept apart from calcium in time; a pharmacist can check yours.
A history of kidney stones, kidney disease or high blood calcium is a reason to talk to a doctor before using calcium supplements.
